consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Oh, I'm so worried about his eyesight. He sits way too close to the TV when watching cartoons and also when reading books. I've tried to get him to move back a bit, but he says he can't see as well then.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Sometimes I call his name and he doesn't respond right away. It's like he's not hearing me or maybe just ignoring me? But if I go over to him and say it again، he'll usually answer. I don't know if it's his hearing or just him being a bit distracted.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: His teeth are a worry for me because the dentist said the enamel is weak. We have to be super careful with sugary foods and make sure he brushes them really well to prevent cavities.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: When he plays outside with friends， his breathing gets much faster than the other kids. Even when they're all running around together， my son seems to be panting more. I've mentioned it to his dad， but we haven't done anything about it yet.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Poor baby... he has low muscle tone. The physiotherapist is working with him to improve it. You can see it when he walks or tries to hold things; it's just a bit more effortful for him than for other kids his age.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Eating can be tricky sometimes. He's super fussy about food textures and won't eat certain things because of how they feel in his mouth. Like， mashed potatoes are okay but not if they're lumpy at all.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Yes... his fingers are shorter than usual. We were told it's just something he was born with and doesn't affect anything else.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a heart condition, specifically changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has trouble eating, preferring mashed potatoes over lumpy foods.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has low muscle tone, requiring physical therapy to improve it.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has trouble seeing clearly, particularly when called by name.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has trouble seeing clearly, particularly when called by name.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has shorter-than-average fingers.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs to be extra cautious with sugary foods and ensure proper toothbrushing to prevent cavities.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has behavioral differences, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient needs to be extra cautious with sugary foods and ensure proper toothbrushing to prevent cavities.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient should have regular hearing checks to age 5, even if earlier reviews give a clear response.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient should have regular eye exams to check for vision problems.
d) Check position of testes in boys: The patient's testes should be checked to rule out cryptorchidism.
e) Consider a palate review: The patient should be referred for a palate review if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.
f) Referral for a cardiac review: The patient should undergo a cardiac review, including echocardiography and electrocardiogram, following diagnosis.
g) If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated.
h) Consider a skeletal review: The patient should have X-rays of the wrist, hips, spine, and skull to assess bone age and detect any abnormalities.
i) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review.
j) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord: The patient should be evaluated for tethered cord if clinical concerns arise, especially if a sacral dimple is present.
k) Monitor growth velocity: The patient's height should be monitored closely, and if it falls below the 2nd centile, referral for endocrine investigations should be considered.
l) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: The patient may benefit from various therapies depending on their specific needs.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences fatigue and difficulty maintaining physical activity, indicating potential cardiovascular issues.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including valve changes, hole in the heart chambers, and structural abnormalities, which can lead to reduced strength and endurance.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has bowel problems, experiencing accidents and struggles with going to the bathroom, requiring assistance with toileting.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, leading to conductive hearing loss and speech delays.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which can be managed with standard anti-epileptic medications.

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits hypotonia, affecting muscle tone and making movement and self-care more challenging.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Hypotonia is a common feature in KBG syndrome, contributing to reduced strength and coordination.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty focusing on distant objects, suggesting possible visual processing issues.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Myopia, or near-sightedness, is a common issue among people with KBG syndrome, impacting their ability to see clearly at a distance.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems, specifically astigmatism and short- or long-sightedness, which can impact reading and social interactions.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Astigmatism and short- or long-sightedness are frequent complications in KBG syndrome, potentially affecting communication and social engagement.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has tooth sensitivity and breaks or chips easily, necessitating careful handling of food and toys.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Tooth sensitivity and susceptibility to damage are common in KBG syndrome, increasing the risk of cavities and fractures.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires additional support in school, particularly in areas like handwriting, dressing, and personal hygiene.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome often need extra help in school, with some attending specialized schools or receiving EHCPs.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient shows behavioral differences, possibly including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Behavioral differences are common in KBG syndrome, with some children exhibiting ASD, ADHD, or anxiety.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, leading to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including structural abnormalities, which can contribute to spinal curvature.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: To prevent tooth decay and maintain proper oral health.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: To detect and address hearing impairments early.
c) Ophthalmology review: To monitor vision and address any vision-related issues.
d) Palate review: To assess speech and feeding capabilities, especially if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.
e) Cardiac review: Including echocardiography and electrocardiogram (ECG) to rule out heart conditions.
f) Skeletal review: X-rays of the wrist, hips, spine, and skull to evaluate bone age and identify any structural abnormalities.
g) Monitoring growth velocity: To track height and ensure it remains within normal ranges.
h) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: To provide comprehensive support for various aspects of development and daily living.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences fatigue quickly, needing to rest after short playtimes at the park compared to her peers.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient struggles with feeding, requiring short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds. Lack of interest in feeding can be significant and long-lasting.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have swallowing difficulties, leading to choking and aspiration pneumonia.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an issue with her spinal cord being tethered, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient rubs her eyes quite often, especially when focusing on something, and picks up on certain sounds but not others.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have hearing problems, including recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and treatment can include patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery to bring the eyes into line.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have hearing problems, including recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has tooth sensitivity, particularly with cold foods like ice cream or frozen yogurt, making it a challenge to find toothpaste she can tolerate.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have tooth sensitivity, making it a challenge to find toothpaste they can tolerate.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school. The extra demands of mainstream secondary school may prove too challenging, and children may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have hearing problems, including recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety. Medication(s) may be appropriate in some circumstances.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis). Babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle). Many people with KBG syndrome have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient has tooth sensitivity, especially with cold foods, making it a challenge to find toothpaste she can tolerate.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5 (even if earlier reviews give a clear response): The patient has hearing problems, including recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and treatment can include patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery to bring the eyes into line.
d) Palate review: The patient has subtler anomalies affecting speech development and feeding, potentially referring for specialist review.
e) Cardiac review (including echocardiogram and electrocardiogram) following diagnosis: The patient experiences fatigue quickly, needing to rest after short playtimes at the park compared to her peers.
f) Tethered cord MRI: One study found that 11% of children with KBG syndrome have tethered cord, which means that the spinal cord cannot move freely. This can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait. Most children with KBG syndrome do not have these issues.
g) Monitoring growth velocity: If the patient's height is below the 2nd centile, refer for endocrine investigations within the context of familial heights.
h) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: The patient has difficulty getting the words out clearly, and sometimes catches herself struggling to find the right thing to say.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Well, we've noticed he seems to hear some sounds but not others clearly. For instance, if we're watching TV together, he'll respond to loud noises but sometimes doesn't react to softer voices or certain tones. It's like he's picking and choosing what he wants to listen to, but I'm not sure if that's normal or not.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: He's been complaining about tooth sensitivity lately, especially when he eats cold food like ice cream or cold drinks. He says it hurts and makes him jump. We've tried using special toothpaste, but it doesn't seem to make much difference.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Yes... the doctors found a septal defect. They said it's a hole in the heart that didn't close properly after birth. We go for regular check-ups to monitor it and make sure it doesn't cause more serious problems. It's been a worry for us since the diagnosis.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: He has these episodes where he just stares off into space. It's like he's in a trance or something. We call them his 'blank spells'. They can happen anytime - during play, while eating... it's really frightening because we never know when they'll happen. And sometimes he gets rigid and unresponsive for a few seconds before snapping back to reality.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Constipation has been an issue for him. He struggles to go to the bathroom regularly and when he does, it's often very painful for him. We've tried changing his diet and encouraging more fluid intake but nothing seems to work consistently.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: There are two main things. Firstly, the delayed fontanelle closure has been a concern since birth. The doctors have been monitoring it closely to ensure it doesn't lead to further complications. Secondly, he struggles with clarity when trying to talk. His words aren't always clear, and he gets frustrated when we can't understand him. It's heartbreaking to see him try so hard to communicate but not being able to express himself properly.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits episodes of staring off into space, known as blank spells, which can last for several seconds and are potentially concerning.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, a soft spot on the baby's head, which requires ongoing monitoring to prevent complications.

Parent: N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, leading to conductive hearing loss, where sounds are unable to pass into the inner ear. Many children have required multiple aeration tube (grommet) insertions to relieve pressure inside the ear, and some have still required hearing aids.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits moments where he stares off into space for a few seconds, appearing to be unresponsive during those times.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a structural heart abnormality discovered by the cardiologist, which requires ongoing management and understanding of its potential impact on long-term health.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Monitoring and possible intervention based on the severity of the condition are recommended.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient is described as being very picky with food textures, leading to challenges with mealtime.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many people with KBG syndrome have difficulty swallowing and eating certain textures, which can lead to nutritional deficiencies and delayed growth.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has seizures, which are managed with neurologists' efforts.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which can be treated with standard antiepileptic medications. However, in some cases, treatment may be challenging.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences occasional squinting when looking at things and has difficulty with speech due to feeding difficulties.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many people with KBG syndrome have vision problems such as astigmatism and short-sightedness (myopia/hypermetropia), which can worsen speech delay. Additionally, some have suboptimal palate development affecting speech and feeding.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has squint (strabismus) and may have vision problems such as astigmatism and short-sightedness (myopia/hypermetropia).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have vision problems, including astigmatism and short-sightedness, which can affect speech development and feeding.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have brachydactyly, characterized by shortened fingers with a curvature of the fifth finger.

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has tooth sensitivity, particularly with cold foods, and complaints about tooth sensitivity.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have dental concerns, including weak enamel and sensitive teeth, requiring regular dental check-ups.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome require additional support in school, especially in areas like speech and feeding.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome exhibit behavioral differences, including ASD, ADHD, and anxiety.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have an unusual structure of their spinal bones, resulting in an increased curvature of the spine.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient should have regular dental check-ups to maintain oral health and prevent complications.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient should undergo regular hearing reviews to ensure proper hearing and address any potential issues early.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient should have regular ophthalmology reviews to monitor vision and address any vision-related issues.
d) Palate review: The patient should be referred for a palate review if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.
e) Cardiac review: The patient should undergo a cardiac review, including echocardiography and electrocardiogram, to assess the heart condition and manage any associated issues.
f) Tethered cord review: The patient should be considered for a tethered cord review if clinical concerns arise, particularly if sacral dimple is present.
g) Growth monitoring: The patient's growth velocity should be monitored closely, especially if height is below the 2nd centile, to rule out underlying hormonal imbalances or other growth-related issues.

Parent: Chewing can be hard for her. There are some foods she just can't manage because they're too tough. We try to cut them up small or cook them softer.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Chewing harder foods like apples or meat can be challenging for her. She tends to avoid those types of food altogether because it causes her discomfort. We've considered consulting an orthodontist to assess her bite and jaw alignment.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Physically demanding activities leave her exhausted quickly. While her peers can run around and play without stopping, our daughter needs to take breaks after just a few minutes of moderate exercise. This discrepancy worries us about potential cardiac issues that could impact her quality of life.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Coordination seems to be an issue; simple tasks that require balance and movement are more difficult for her than they should be at her age. Watching her try to navigate playground equipment or even just walk in a straight line shows us that something is off.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Constipation has become a recurring problem. Some days are worse than others‚ but overall‚ she experiences difficulty passing stool regularly. Dietary changes haven't seemed to make a significant difference yet.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: She was diagnosed with scoliosis‚ which affects her posture and gait. Regular monitoring and physiotherapy have been recommended to manage the condition effectively and prevent further complications.
